1.2.1.2-f100.accuracy_reason: Psalm 90(91):6 in the Vulgate has 'daemonio meridiano', the noonday demon, and the gloss matches Burton's 'noonday'.

1.2.1.2-f102.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Caligula 59, reads 'nullam noctem sine aliquo terrore transactam, donec ipsa domus incendio consumpta sit'.

1.2.1.2-f119.accuracy_reason: The sidenote does end with 'lege' and then lists the authorities (Epiphanius, Dionysius, Ambrose and so on), so the description is correct.

1.2.1.2-f12.accuracy_reason: Socrates' daimonion is rightly identified, and Saturn was the planet tied to both melancholy and contemplation.

1.2.1.2-f131.accuracy_reason: The full line in Ovid (Tristia 1.2.4) is 'saepe premente deo fert deus alter opem', so Burton does leave out 'saepe'.

1.2.1.2-f137.accuracy_reason: The Saturn and Jupiter types are described correctly, and Burton's English ('shall never likely be preferred') does draw a consequence rather than translate.

1.2.1.2-f15.accuracy_reason: The note quotes Apuleius, De deo Socratis 13, correctly. Burton's order ('animo passiva, mente rationalia') actually matches Augustine's quotation of it in De civitate Dei 8.16, which the note doesn't mention, but nothing it says is false.

1.2.1.2-f154.accuracy_reason: The Tertullian link (Apologeticus 22) is right. The note also says 'membra distorquent' is close to a Lipsius sidenote, but I can't confirm that from the text given. The phrase 'irrepentes corporibus occulte… membra distorquent' comes from Minucius Felix, Octavius 27 (and Cyprian, Quod idola 7), so that is the likelier source.

1.2.1.2-f188.accuracy_reason: In the Suda, Pases' magic half-obol comes back to him after he spends it, as the note says.

1.2.1.2-f206.accuracy_reason: Weyer's Pseudomonarchia daemonum was printed with the 1577 edition of De praestigiis daemonum, and Burton does write the singular 'Daemonis'.

1.2.1.2-f208.accuracy_reason: Genii were indeed attendant or guardian spirits of persons and places.

1.2.1.2-f209.accuracy_reason: The Manes were the spirits of the dead in Roman religion.

1.2.1.2-f211.accuracy_reason: The text itself places daemones as intermediates between gods and men, which is the Platonic sense.

1.2.1.2-f213.accuracy_reason: The line is Aeneid 4.489, where it describes the Massylian priestess; 'fluvis' is a slip for 'fluviis'; and Burton does attach it to Canidia.

1.2.1.2-f214.accuracy_reason: Ignes fatui is the standard Latin term for will-o'-the-wisps.

1.2.1.2-f242.accuracy_reason: Nyslott (Olavinlinna) in Swedish Finland is the usual identification, and the note rightly says it is uncertain.

1.2.1.2-f271.accuracy_reason: 'Substantiae separatae' is the scholastic term for incorporeal intelligences, that is, angels.

1.2.1.2-f272.accuracy_reason: In De natura deorum 1.60 Cotta says he could sooner say what a god is not than what it is.

1.2.1.2-f279.accuracy_reason: Octavius 10.4: Caecilius, the pagan speaker, mocks the Jewish god as captive with his nation to the Roman deities.

1.2.1.2-f285.accuracy_reason: Ficino's Latin Proclus 'De anima et daemone' existed (in the 1497 Aldine volume). Burton's main text names Proclus, and Symposium 202e is the right passage on daemons as intermediaries; the identification is suitably hedged.

1.2.1.2-f297.accuracy_reason: 'Complexion' is rightly glossed as temperament, and Burton's English does render only the proximate-cause clause, calling it 'choler adust'.

1.2.1.2-f299.accuracy_reason: Plutarch, De defectu oraculorum 415c, preserves Hesiod's riddle with nymphs living ten phoenix-generations; the guess about the numbers is hedged.

1.2.1.2-f304.accuracy_reason: In this context the word is correctly glossed as the personal attendant spirit, as distinct from the Christian 'demon'.

1.2.1.2-f306.accuracy_reason: Lamiae were classical child-devouring and seducing female spectres.

1.2.1.2-f5.accuracy_reason: The senses of acies are right, the link to 'owl's eyes' is fair, and Fracastoro and Fernel are correctly identified.

1.2.1.2-f60.accuracy_reason: Porphyry, Life of Plotinus 10, tells how an Egyptian priest summoned Plotinus' spirit at the Iseum in Rome, and a god appeared rather than a daemon.

1.2.1.2-f62.accuracy_reason: Vulgate Rev. 7:2: 'quattuor angelis quibus datum est nocere terrae et mari' – correctly identified.

1.2.1.2-f64.accuracy_reason: In Civ. Dei 7.6 Varro puts ethereal souls from the highest heaven down to the moon, and aerial souls (heroes, lares, genii) between the moon and the clouds; the note describes Burton's conflation correctly.

1.2.1.2-f65.accuracy_reason: Burton's 'Gazaeus cited by Lipsius' (Physiologia Stoicorum) is Aeneas of Gaza, author of the dialogue Theophrastus; the identification is standard.

1.2.1.2-f66.accuracy_reason: The lines are from Palingenius' Zodiacus Vitae, and Burton's quotation does break off with a dash.

1.2.1.2-f7.accuracy_reason: 'In veritate non stetit' is the Vulgate wording of John 8:44, about the devil.

1.2.1.2-f76.accuracy_reason: Ecl. 8.69 reads 'carmina vel caelo possunt deducere lunam'; Burton's ablative 'Carminibus' does make the spells the instrument.

1.2.1.2-f86.accuracy_reason: Henricus Kornmannus wrote De miraculis mortuorum (1610); the gloss on tripudium is right.
